stories.Headline: Anthropic sued by major Canadian news publishers for copyright claims in Ontario court
stories.Summary:
A group of Canada’s largest news publishers, including Postmedia, Torstar, The Globe and Mail, and The Canadian Press, filed a copyright lawsuit against the AI company Anthropic in an Ontario court on October 6, 2026. The publishers claim Anthropic used their content without a valid license to develop its large language AI model, Claude. They allege the company scraped their websites, bypassing technological protections to copy large volumes of text data. The lawsuit says Anthropic has been substantially and unjustly enriched at the publishers’ expense. Anthropic has not yet responded to the claims, and the allegations have not been proven in court.

The statement of claim says Anthropic breached the news media websites’ terms of service and circumvented technological protection measures meant to restrict copying. The publishers say they are responsible for generating a significant portion of Canada’s journalistic content, from daily print broadsheets to round-the-clock digital news coverage, and collectively have millions of readers. The claim states that Anthropic deliberately scrapes enormous amounts of text data from the internet and from the plaintiffs’ websites, then uses that content without authorization or consent to develop its AI models. It also says Anthropic scrapes content on an ongoing basis in response to user prompts. The lawsuit was first reported by the news site Cartt.ca.

The news publishers argue that Anthropic has capitalized on the commercial success of its AI models, built an expansive suite of services, and raised significant capital, all without obtaining a valid licence from any of the news media companies. They say Anthropic has done nothing to curtail its unlawful behaviour despite concerns raised by content creators across various industries, including through numerous other lawsuits and public criticism. Anthropic has not responded to a request for comment. The same companies, alongside CBC/Radio-Canada, also launched a lawsuit against OpenAI in 2024, and that case has yet to be settled.

News publishers have been pushing the federal government to take a stand on how AI systems use copyrighted content after the government’s national AI strategy failed to address the issue. The case is currently pending in Ontario court. If successful, the lawsuit might lead to stricter regulations on how AI models can use copyrighted material in Canada, potentially impacting AI companies’ operations and development processes. The legal action could set a precedent for how AI companies must engage with content creators. No further court dates or next steps were provided in the articles.

stories.Headline: AI and neocloud stock sell-off is in headlines, but expert warns artificial intelligence demand is the hidden factor no one is watching
stories.Summary:
A sharp sell-off in artificial intelligence and neocloud stocks has drawn headlines, but one expert says the real story is hidden demand. The market decline happened in late October 2026, with big tech facing a major reality check as volatile markets, rising oil prices, and massive spending on AI tested investors’ patience. Josh Schafer, Barron’s Investor Circle Newsletter Editor and FOX Business Contributor, discussed the situation on FBN with Taylor Riggs. They examined whether the current tech market resembles the 1999 dot-com bubble or the 2023 regional banking scare.

The discussion highlighted under-the-radar stocks benefiting from data center expansion, suggesting that the sell-off may not reflect weakening AI demand. Schafer warned that artificial intelligence demand is the hidden factor no one is watching, implying that the underlying need for computing power remains strong even as share prices fall. The articles did not provide specific numbers, dates, or names beyond the October 19, 2026 publication date and the individuals already mentioned. No new regulatory requirements or policy changes were described.

Josh Schafer and Taylor Riggs analyzed the AI stock boom and its recent decline. Schafer’s comments, as paraphrased, indicate that investors are impatient with heavy AI spending, but the demand driving that spending has not disappeared. They also reacted to Elon Musk’s proposal to give SpaceX stock to American children, though no further details on that proposal were included. The conversation framed the sell-off as a test of investor patience rather than a collapse in AI usage.

The context is a broader debate about whether the AI investment cycle is a bubble or a durable expansion. The articles compare the moment to past financial scares, but they do not state what happens next. No future dates, policy decisions, or company actions are given. Because the available reporting offers analysis rather than new developments, this is a breaking story. More to follow.

stories.Headline: World brings biometric proof of human to banking and AI agents
stories.Summary:
World introduced biometric proof of personhood for banking and financial services on October 19, 2026 at Money20/20 in Las Vegas. Tools for Humanity CEO and World co-founder Alex Blania unveiled World ID for banking and finance on stage. The offering combines three products, the World ID app, World ID for Zoom and World ID for Agents. All three use cryptographic proofs to establish whether someone is a unique human, whether they are present in the moment, and specific identity attributes such as age or nationality.

The World ID app is available through the App Store and Google Play in more than 150 countries. Proof of Human requires a one-time visit to a World Orb, and Orbs are also available at the New York Stock Exchange. Proof of Presence uses a smartphone liveness check and does not require Orb verification. Proof of Attributes confirms information from an official government credential, such as nationality or being over a certain age, while revealing only the requested information. World says financial institutions can use these proofs when customers visit branches, open accounts, transfer significant sums or recover access to their accounts.

Bain Capital, OpenExchange, Outtake, Pantera Capital and VanEck Funds are the initial design partners, and no bank is among the named partners. Blania said the company believed the future would be agentic, and that a proof of human would become the gate for almost any transaction on the internet. World says automated traffic surpassed human traffic on the web for the first time this year. The company cites Deloitte estimates that generative AI-enabled fraud losses in the United States could reach $40 billion by 2027, up from an estimated $12.3 billion in 2023.

World ID for Zoom is designed for high-stakes interactions including transaction approvals, investment discussions and merger negotiations. Participants first complete a one-time biometric verification at a World Orb and connect their World ID to Zoom, then a live selfie confirms the participant matches the previously verified individual. A Human Badge appears on the participant's Zoom tile, and meeting hosts will soon be able to require verification in a Zoom waiting room before admitting attendees. World says Zoom receives no personal information during verification. World ID for Agents uses AgentKit, a suite of developer tools currently in beta that allows individuals to delegate cryptographic proofs to AI agents.

stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq 100’s rebound is about to be tested by earnings from Meta and Tesla, which report third-quarter 2026 results after the US close on Monday. The index rose 1.1% on Thursday and added just 0.067% on Friday to close at 29,549.02 points, a muted follow-through that suggests investors are buying the dip without committing to it. Amazon made the largest single contribution to Thursday’s recovery, with Nvidia, Tesla and Alphabet also lending support. The buying followed the previous week’s selloff ahead of major corporate results rather than any fresh fundamental catalyst. A Jefferies analysis put net sales of US technology stocks in the previous week at USD 7.5 billion, the highest level in five years.

Meta and Tesla face high expectations because investors want evidence that heavy AI spending is converting into revenue growth and profitability. At Meta, the focus falls on whether incremental revenue can absorb capital outlays, since simply reaffirming ambitious investment plans would leave the funding question unanswered. Tesla faces a sharper numeric hurdle, with analyst consensus cited by Reuters pointing to revenue of about USD 27.88 billion and adjusted earnings of roughly USD 0.43 per share, alongside negative free cash flow of USD 4.92 billion. Stronger deliveries must show up in the financials, not just in the delivery headline. Citigroup expects the technology sector to account for nearly 70% of global earnings growth next year, which shows how concentrated profit expectations have become.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh declined on Friday to signal how the next rate decision will go, saying the economy had largely developed as expected since September’s hike but offering no direction for the coming vote. The next policy meeting runs 27, 28 October, meaning the Fed question and the earnings question will be settled in the same window. The pressure on valuations traces back to prices, since US consumer prices rose 0.6% month-on-month in September and 3.7% year-on-year, reinforcing expectations of further rate hikes. Final-demand producer prices climbed 1.3% in September from the prior month and 6.3% from a year earlier, hardening the case that monetary policy will stay restrictive.

The stakes extend well beyond two companies because the Nasdaq 100’s advance is still unconfirmed and the Fed’s October verdict is pending. The coming week’s reports must do more than ride the rebound, since they need to draw a credible line between investment and return. Persistent volatility in AI-linked names capped the upside for the tech sector, even though the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index ended its longest losing streak since 2008 during Thursday’s session. That technical milestone says more about the length of the prior slide than about the strength of the recovery. With the earnings question and the Fed decision landing in the same window, investors will learn whether the rebound has a fundamental basis or remains a short-term bounce.

stories.Headline: AUS to host world's only UNESCO Chair in Arabic, AI and Digital Heritage
stories.Summary:
The American University of Sharjah has signed an agreement with UNESCO to establish a UNESCO Chair in Arabic Language, Artificial Intelligence and Digital Heritage. The agreement was made under the patronage of Sheikha Bodour bint Sultan Al Qasimi, President and Chairperson of the Board of Trustees of AUS. This makes AUS the only university in the world to host a UNESCO Chair of this kind. The announcement was reported on October 19, 2026. The Chair will support cultural preservation through high-tech solutions and expand access to Arabic language and heritage.

Its objectives include collecting, digitising and curating artefacts, including endangered Arabic dialects, through digital tools and multilingual metadata standards. It will advance interdisciplinary research by integrating AI, machine learning and digital tools to produce scholarly publications and open-access resources. The Chair will also build regional capacity through workshops, certification programmes and opportunities for early-career scholars, media professionals and cultural practitioners. It will strengthen collaboration with institutions in the Arab States, Africa and Asia-Pacific and with UNESCO networks, while engaging youth in digital storytelling.

Dr Tod A. Laursen, Chancellor of AUS, said Arabic carries the memory of a region, its ideas, its poetry and its everyday voices. He said that when archives remain undigitised or dialects go undocumented, heritage becomes harder to reach and easier to lose. He added that the Chair reflects Sharjah’s enduring commitment to culture and knowledge. Irakli Khodeli, Chief of Management of Social Transformations and Foresight Section at UNESCO, said the Arabic language is used daily by more than 500 million people.

He said UNESCO and its Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz Al Saud Programme for the Arabic Language are delighted to join forces with the new Chair. The Chair will be grounded in existing strengths at AUS, including the Centre for Arab Studies and Islamic Civilizations and the Department of Arabic and Translation Studies. AUS was founded in 1997 by His Highness Dr Sheikh Sultan Bin Mohammed Al Qasimi, Ruler of Sharjah. The Chair will work closely with UNESCO, other UNESCO Chairs and the University Twinning and Networking Programme, known as UNITWIN, on relevant programmes and activities.

stories.Headline: Nexus-CLI – Pure Go Bridge to DeepSeek R1/V3 with Claude Code and Ollama Support
stories.Summary:
On October 21, 2026, a developer known as xamrayev published Nexus-CLI on GitHub, a command line tool written in pure Go. It acts as a bridge that lets any application or coding agent connect to DeepSeek V3 and R1 models through a free web account at chat.deepseek.com, without needing a paid official API key. The project was rewritten from scratch based on analysis of earlier Node.js and Python projects, and it has zero runtime dependencies. It includes a parallel proof of work solver that handles difficulty 144,000 challenges in about 40 to 50 milliseconds.

The tool requires Go 1.20 or newer to build, and users can install it by cloning the repository, running go build, or using go install. Authentication can be done three ways: an interactive login that asks for a userToken from browser local storage, an automatic Chrome method using CDP, or a .env file with a DEEPSEEK_TOKEN value. Nexus-CLI provides an interactive terminal chat, one off prompts, Unix pipe support, and a local proxy server on port 9655 by default. It offers OpenAI, Anthropic, and Ollama compatible endpoints, including POST /v1/chat/completions, POST /v1/messages, POST /v1/responses, GET /v1/models, and Ollama routes like GET /api/tags and POST /api/chat. It also supports structured JSON output, multi-account rotation to avoid HTTP 429 rate limits, and a doctor command for diagnostics.

The developer, xamrayev, wrote the documentation in English, Russian, and Uzbek, and distributed the code under the MIT License. The README explains that the tool solves DeepSeek server challenges using the DeepSeekHashV1 algorithm, which is based on Keccak-f[1600] with 1 to 23 rounds of SHA3-256. It also describes launchers for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Goose, Aider, and other tools, with Nexus automatically booting the proxy in the background. The project structure lists files for the proof of work solver, stream parser, authentication manager, Chrome authentication, HTTP proxy server, and launcher.

The GitHub repository had 3 stars, 0 watchers, and 0 forks at the time of publication. Separately, on October 19, 2026, Techmeme reported that developers and vibe coders were using AI tools like Claude Code to remove sponsored ads from smart TVs and disable tracking features. That same day, the US Department of Homeland Security ordered all federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek technology from their IT systems and prohibited future procurement of its products and services. The order also covered third party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations, according to multiple news outlets.

stories.Headline: AI becomes key issue in U.S. midterm elections, from data centers to jobs
stories.Summary:
Ahead of the November midterm elections, regulation and oversight of the AI industry have become major political issues in the United States. On Oct. 19, The Verge reported that leading Democratic lawmakers signaled they could closely investigate tax credits related to data centers and recent cybersecurity incidents if their party wins a majority in either the House or the Senate. That would allow them to call AI company chief executives to testify and demand internal documents. Voter interest is growing because of concerns about power consumption, environmental burdens tied to data center construction, and fears of job losses.

The debate involves specific proposals and large sums of money. Ideas mentioned within and outside the Democratic Party include pre-deployment safety testing for advanced AI models, child protection, stronger corporate accountability for labour and housing discrimination, and requiring companies to pay part of the costs of job displacement caused by AI. Rob Flaherty, a former deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris, recently set up the political action committee Tomorrow Together and launched a $4 million advertising campaign targeting Republican candidates. By contrast, the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future had spent about $45 million as of June and held $31 million in funds. In Virginia, the data processing and computer services sector gave $372,000 since Jan. 1, 2025, to 10 congressional and Senate candidates, with almost four of every five dollars going to Democrats, according to OpenSecrets.org.

Several people commented on the political shift. Democratic strategist Jesse Lehrich called it an opportunity for AI regulation to gain political attention but said it was uncertain whether Democrats would turn that into actual policy. Rob Flaherty said Democrats had long failed to address AI issues aggressively, citing a lack of understanding of technology and the AI industry's massive political funding. Mark Rozell, a political science professor at George Mason University, said the issue is not going away and will have an impact on elections in Virginia and nationally. Elena Schlossberg of the Coalition to Protect Prince William County said community after community finally woke up, and she warned candidates that if they run and win on this issue but do not produce results, they will not win again.

Public opinion has shifted sharply. A statewide poll of 1,101 registered Virginia voters at the end of March by the Schar School and the Washington Post showed only 35 percent were comfortable with a data center in their communities, down from 69 percent in 2023. Localities including Prince William, Fauquier, Loudoun and Carroll counties are denying, delaying or limiting data center construction. The coalition recently prevailed over plans to develop the 2,000-acre Dulles Cloud South project, which would have packed 4.3 million square feet of computer servers into a structure several stories tall, making it the largest such facility on earth. Observers say the direction of regulation for the U.S. AI industry could shift depending on the balance of power in Congress after the midterms.

stories.Headline: Nvidia RTX Spark Brings Local AI Agents to Windows Laptops
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced on Oct. 16 that its RTX Spark Windows laptops were available, bringing local AI models and agents to compatible devices. The laptops are sold by Asus, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft, and MSI, starting at $2,599. The RTX Spark is a single chip combining an Nvidia Blackwell RTX GPU and an Nvidia Grace CPU, with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. Nvidia also provides native CUDA support and AI models such as the Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B, a 74-billion-parameter model, and advertises support for models with up to 120 billion parameters.

The Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark edition, model H7607, starts at $2,799.99 with an 18-core RTX Spark N1X chip, 24GB of unified memory, and 512GB of SSD storage. A Best Buy model with 32GB of memory and 1TB of storage costs $3,399.99. A configuration with a 20-core Grace CPU, 6,144-CUDA-core Blackwell GPU, 64GB of memory, and 1TB SSD is available for $4,399.99. The top-tier Asus model has a 4K OLED touch screen, 128GB of LPDDR5X memory, 2TB of storage, and the 20-core chip, selling for $6,999.99. The laptop includes a 16-inch OLED display, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4, and a bundled Asus ProArt Mouse MD301 priced at $99.

Microsoft executive vice president Yusuf Mehdi said the company is building Windows to be the platform for hybrid intelligence, where AI can run locally when it makes sense and reach the cloud when needed. Microsoft provides Windows and development tools, including Windows Subsystem for Linux, native Python support, and PyTorch with CUDA for Windows on Arm. IT teams should test required applications, Python packages, model runtimes, and endpoint-management tools before buying Windows on Arm hardware. Local inference gives more control over processing but does not automatically guarantee privacy, because connected tools, telemetry, and cloud fallbacks may still transmit information externally.

The RTX Spark platform is intended to let developers handle more coding, testing, and prototyping locally while keeping cloud resources for larger workloads, including trillion-parameter AI models. PCMag began first tests on the Asus ProArt P16, noting that gaming performance at 1080p and 1200p resolutions was playable in games like Cyberpunk 2077, with CUDA-core counts matching a desktop GeForce RTX 5070. Availability and pricing in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Egypt were not confirmed at the time of the review. IT teams are advised to start with a limited pilot using representative tasks and approved data, then measure compatibility, task quality, response times, and remaining cloud usage before deciding on wider purchases.

stories.Headline: Wuzhen Summit Puts Spotlight on Tongxiang's Expanding AI Industry
stories.Summary:
The 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit will open on Nov. 2, bringing technology leaders, researchers and companies to the historic water town. Ahead of the event, reporters visited seven Tongxiang-based companies working in robotics, intelligent vehicles, synthetic data, industrial automation, logistics and computing infrastructure. These firms are expanding AI applications from commercial cleaning and autonomous delivery to industrial control and data-center cooling. The summit is a chance to demonstrate how local companies are commercializing AI technologies for customers at home and abroad.

CenoBots, a Tongxiang-based company, has sold cleaning robots in more than 40 countries and regions, with customers including Changi Airport, Tesco, the University of Minnesota and Novo Nordisk. This year, the company supplied about 600 autonomous cleaning robots for Tesco Express stores across the United Kingdom. CenoBots has expanded its research, development and production facilities in Tongxiang from approximately 3,000 square meters in its early years to more than 20,000 square meters. TEEMO makes drive-by-wire skateboard chassis and core components for autonomous vehicles used in last-mile delivery, patrols and logistics, and its customers span the United States, the Middle East, India and Russia. Dayan Technology, founded in Tongxiang in May 2025, provides synthetic-data and toolchain services for autonomous-driving and humanoid-robotics companies.

Freetech develops intelligent-driving systems and 4D imaging radar for passenger and commercial vehicles, and its technology has been selected for hundreds of vehicle programs. At its intelligent-manufacturing base in Wuzhen, an in-house AI system reads customer orders and calculates components and materials needed for each production line, increasing overall efficiency by more than 20%. Shuhan Technologies, founded in 2019, provides on-premises industrial AI for chemical plants, energy facilities and wastewater-treatment systems. At a coal chemical plant with annual capacity of 1.2 million metric tons, Shuhan said its system reduced raw-material consumption by 6% and generated more than 176 million yuan, or about $26 million, in annualized economic benefits, while reducing carbon emissions by more than 500,000 metric tons. SynthCool develops two-phase liquid-cooling systems that support heat dissipation of more than 3,000 watts per chip and heat flux above 250 watts per square centimeter.

CenoBots co-founder and vice president Shen Jizhong said cleaning robots are appearing in more settings, much like electric vehicles becoming a familiar sight on the roads. TEEMO director of operations Zhang Yongjian said autonomous delivery vehicles have strong potential in overseas markets where distances are long and last-mile delivery is difficult to staff. Freetech founder and CEO Dr. Zhang Lin said transportation combined with a specialized function will be an important direction for the future, with potential applications including robots, elder-care vehicles, mining equipment and agricultural machinery. Shuhan Chief Technology Officer Zhai Zhengjun said all industrial process challenges can be framed as control and optimization problems. SynthCool general manager Zhu Zhijiang said heat dissipation is infrastructure.

stories.Headline: AI challenges math by solving the unsolvable
stories.Summary:
Since April, artificial intelligence companies have regularly published solutions to previously unsolved mathematical problems. Last week, OpenAI released solutions to 719 previously unsolved problems. Hugo Duminil-Copin, winner of the 2022 Fields Medal, told colleagues at the French Mathematical Society that all his avenues of research are now gone. Richie Sater, a 32 year old CPA and technology entrepreneur, recently used AI agents he built to solve a problem that a Belarusian mathematician entered into a repository for unsolved problems in 1986. The problem, Problem 10.34 in the Kourovka Notebook, concerned finite groups that are the product of every pair of non-conjugate maximal subgroups being soluble.

Sater’s AI agents took about three weeks to solve the problem, and he then contacted mathematician Viktor Monakhov with an answer and supporting materials. Sater put together an audit package so mathematicians could quickly review the work instead of spending two weeks checking every claimed answer. Monakhov endorsed the work and sent it to peer review, then gave Sater another problem, which he also solved. Sater said the last two problems took about three days instead of three weeks for his AI agents to solve, and he now has several papers submitted for publication.

Stephane Mallat, 2025 Gold Medal recipient from France’s national scientific research center, said mathematics goes far beyond calculation and is a way of thinking clearly. He said maths will remain absolutely central because it allows humans to think clearly and understand things. Mallat also said mathematicians are needed for teaching, and he rejected the idea that researchers will be replaced by AI. Francois Charles, a mathematician and department head at the Ecole Normale Superieure in Paris, said he is not pessimistic on the scientific side, though there are legitimate concerns about how the community is organized. Cedric Villani, 2010 Fields Medalist, said in Le Figaro that in mathematics, the conclusion is less important than the path to get there.

The Simons Foundation, a major American patron of mathematics, announced last week a $15 million program co-funded by OpenAI and Anthropic to support mathematicians in dealing with AI. The program will fund workshops to assess AI results and establish standards for their use. Sater said the math community has a huge reviewer bottleneck and needs more scalable ways to verify AI-generated work, and he sees an opportunity for CPAs to apply assurance skills to AI-generated work in mathematics, financial analysis, and other business processes. He estimated that a CPA with basic computer literacy can start building basic AI agents in about a week.

stories.Headline: Greece Unveils National Supercomputer to Advance Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Greece has unveiled its new national supercomputer, named Daedalus, at the Lavrio Technological and Cultural Park. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Minister of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence Dimitris Papastergiou attended the inauguration ceremony. The system was inaugurated in October 2026, with the first article published on 21 October 2026. It is part of the country’s effort to move from relying on foreign artificial intelligence technologies toward developing its own AI applications.

Daedalus is the most powerful supercomputer ever installed in Greece, with a budget of €58.9 million and performance that places it 31st worldwide. Its measured performance reaches 85.69 petaflops, equivalent to approximately 85.69 quadrillion floating-point operations per second. In the Green500 global ranking of energy-efficient supercomputers, it ranked 23rd in June 2026. The system is based on Nvidia Grace Hopper GH200 technology and uses liquid cooling. With the new system, Greece joins a group of 14 countries worldwide with their own dedicated artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The supercomputer will support scientific research, businesses and the development of new AI-based applications. It will also serve as a core component of the infrastructure of the Pharos AI centre. Research institutions, healthcare providers, public bodies and businesses will be able to use it to develop AI applications on infrastructure located in Greece, subject to applicable security and data protection requirements. Business access to the supercomputer will be supported by Pharos AI Factory, Greece’s AI factory. Under current plans, its services are expected to become generally available to businesses in March 2027.

Mitsotakis said investments in advanced technologies would help improve public services, boost productivity and attract highly skilled professionals and technology companies to Greece. He also highlighted the risks associated with the rapid development of artificial intelligence. He stressed the need for effective oversight of the technology, stronger protection for children and the preservation of human responsibility in decision-making. GRNET is advancing plans for a second supercomputer, to be installed at the University of Western Macedonia, with a budget of €21.57 million including VAT for computing equipment, storage and software.

stories.Headline: Who controls intelligence? Open-weight models, institutional AI
stories.Summary:
Reflection AI released Beam on 5 October 2026, a 501-billion-parameter open-weight model with 23 billion active parameters, built with NVIDIA for science, government and sovereign AI users. The Brooklyn-based lab was founded in March 2024 by former Google DeepMind researchers Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou. Beam was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens in under four weeks using 6,144 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs, with reinforcement learning generating more than 100 million rollouts on 10,500 of the same GPUs. Reflection AI says Beam matches GLM 5.2 on advanced reasoning benchmarks while using three to four times less inference compute.

The weights were released under an open-source Apache 2.0 license, with tools for running and fine-tuning the model available on Hugging Face. Reflection AI had not released a public model until October 2026, despite raising billions and signing compute deals worth up to US$7 billion. The company is the AI model provider for the US Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, which serves the 17 US National Laboratories. Its Series B round in October 2025 raised US$2 billion at an US$8 billion valuation, including US$800 million from NVIDIA, and a later Series C closed at a US$25 billion pre-money valuation.

Misha Laskin, co-founder and CEO, said you cannot do scientific discovery on a closed model, comparing it to doing rocket science where you only get to look at the rocket instead of taking it apart and examining the engine. He said governments, scientists and enterprises are looking for frontier AI they can own, inspect and run themselves. The company sought a US-native alternative to Chinese-owned open-weight labs such as DeepSeek. A SpaceX agreement worth up to US$6.3 billion provides GB300 capacity at the Colossus 2 data centre near Memphis, while a Nebius contract worth more than US$1 billion adds more GPUs.

Reflection AI is also building a 250MW data centre joint venture with Shinsegae in South Korea. In Türkiye, the Bilge family of Turkish large language models developed by TÜBITAK Bilgem was unveiled at the Türkiye AI Summit on June 13, 2026, alongside the country's 2026-2030 AI Action Plan, which came into effect on Aug. 18, 2026. The Evren platform, opened for general access in September 2026, processes data on infrastructure located in Türkiye and offers 11 open-weight language models through a single interface. The article says Türkiye's approach should be strengthened by a feedback mechanism that continuously channels data from real-world applications into model development.

stories.Headline: Mass. college students to join nationwide walkout calling for AI regulation
stories.Summary:
Students from at least 10 Massachusetts colleges and universities plan to walk out of class on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, to demand stronger public oversight and regulation of artificial intelligence. The demonstration is part of a nationwide effort organized by Irreplaceable, a group advocating for a freeze on AI development until its risks are better understood. Participants are expected to gather outside the Massachusetts State House from 1 to 3 p.m. that day. Schools involved include Harvard University, MIT, Boston University, Northeastern University, Wellesley College, the University of Massachusetts, and Tufts University.

The walkout calls for a national freeze on AI development and greater public participation in decisions about how the technology is built and regulated. Organizers say major technology companies are developing increasingly powerful AI systems too quickly and without enough public oversight. They also want elected officials in Massachusetts to create legislation regulating rapidly advancing AI technologies. Last month, Governor Maura Healey called for AI safety language and transparency protections in the Mass Wins Act that would encourage independent safety evaluations and stronger reporting requirements for the most powerful AI models.

Ari Rosenthal, lead organizer and co-founder of the Massachusetts AI Action Network, said students have been told college would give them job security, but many now question what the future looks like with this technology. He said a handful of CEOs and executives in Silicon Valley are making unilateral decisions that will shape society. Rosenthal also said the walkout was partly inspired by Jacob Coxon, a researcher who quit his job at Anthropic and accused that company and OpenAI of acting irresponsibly. Coxon said in a post on X that he resigned out of concern that the companies are gambling with people’s lives and that those building AI earnestly believe it could kill everyone by the end of the decade.

Rosenthal said the movement aims to raise awareness about how AI connects to children’s safety, data privacy, and climate change. He described the technology as a black box and said no other area of society would allow this much risk without debate. Irreplaceable organizers said each demonstration will include speakers sharing testimonies about how unregulated AI has affected their lives, jobs, and communities. Rosenthal said he hopes the walkout puts pressure on the Massachusetts legislature to regulate AI and encourages transparency around the governor’s plans to adopt AI within governmental systems.

stories.Headline: Opposition urges N.S. Premier Tim Houston to debate AI data centre in legislature
stories.Summary:
EverWind Fuels announced on Friday that U.S. AI company Anthropic signed a 20 year lease for a $10 billion, 18,600 square metre facility in Point Tupper, Nova Scotia, near Port Hawkesbury. The project would draw 95 megawatts of electricity during its first phase, and EverWind describes it as the largest private investment in provincial history. The Point Tupper project expects to create 2,000 construction jobs and another 215 permanent positions in the centre and its associated wind developments. NDP Leader Claudia Chender wrote to Premier Tim Houston on Monday asking him to recall the legislature for an emergency debate about the proposal.

Chender said the government has embraced AI data centres without public input or establishing regulations. She said data centres have a well documented history of driving up power bills, consuming too much fresh water and harming local communities. As of Monday afternoon, a Change.org petition to stop the development of AI data centres in Nova Scotia had 12,700 signatures, and it was created on Friday. EverWind said the project will cover the cost of all electricity infrastructure and will not increase power rates. The company said the system would use an average of 100,000 litres of water per day in the first phase and an average of 500,000 litres per day when the expansion is complete.

Premier Tim Houston, who also serves as minister of energy, said in an emailed statement Monday that he understands Nova Scotians have questions and concerns. He said this is a first of its kind proposal and there will be many checks and balances built into the process. Late last month, Houston said on social media that any AI data centre in Nova Scotia would have to meet or exceed federal standards for responsible development, including closed loop cooling and strict standards around water use, noise and emissions. Chender responded that non binding guidelines are not laws and the project needs to be regulated in the legislature, not on Facebook. Thomas Arnason McNeil, a senior energy coordinator with the Halifax based Ecology Action Centre, said it is unclear how the project would impact groundwater resources or electricity costs for ratepayers.

A recent United Nations University report says the environmental footprint of data centres globally already rivals some of the world’s largest countries, and it predicts their water and energy use and pollution will double in just four years as use of artificial intelligence grows. Sean Mullin, a senior fellow at the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs, said the AI sector is expanding on a scale society has not seen since the introduction of railways or the Manhattan Project. He said Canada has the space, electricity and water resources to build AI computing capacity properly, but navigating public opposition will depend on how thoughtful and responsible the proponents are. Mullin said proponents who are not transparent and move too quickly are likely to be met with backlash.

stories.Headline: Watchtower, which uses AI and simulation software to help the US Armed Forces make logistical decisions, emerges from stealth with a $35M seed (Alex Konrad/Upstarts Media)
stories.Summary:
Watchtower Labs launched on October 21, 2026, with $35 million in seed funding to help the U.S. Armed Forces make logistical decisions using AI and simulation software. The company was incubated out of Shield Capital, and the funding round was co-led by Shield Capital and Conviction, with participation from In-Q-Tel and Founders Fund. CEO Akhil Iyer, a former Marine Corps special operations combat veteran, founded the company after a meeting in Hawaii with Admiral Samuel Paparo, leader of U.S. Pacific Command. Admiral Paparo told investors that important troop and ship movements were still decided in Excel spreadsheets and emailed around, which led Iyer and Shield Capital founder Raj Shah to build the startup themselves.

The software lets users ask questions in natural language, and locally run large language models find and process the corresponding data to understand the scenario. Watchtower then runs thousands of simulations to return likely contingencies or suggested actions through a custom dashboard or a shareable presentation. The company has a distributed team of nearly 30 people across the Bay Area, Hawaii, Seattle, and Washington, D.C., and already holds several early prototype-style contracts with major operational commands. CTO Suren Aghajanyan and head of engineering John Morman both previously worked as managers at Microsoft, and the company plans to hire more engineers and customer-facing staff with the new funding.

Iyer said the company is building a product that peers into the future at the distribution of outcomes that could be, ideally early enough for users to act. He also said you cannot LLM your way to supply chain optimization, meaning the AI models are only one part of the solution. Conviction partner Sarah Guo said humans using Excel and email is not a reasonable system in the age of superintelligence, and she argued that big AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI are unlikely to build this kind of tool any time soon. Shah said Watchtower's tools could eventually prove valuable in other regulated industries, though the company has no immediate plans to move beyond defense.

The startup is named after Operation Watchtower, the codename for the Guadalcanal campaign during World War II, which Iyer described as an early test for American forces before the U.S. had built up its industrial muscle. Recent reports have detailed warnings of missile shortages and a historically long deployment for the U.S. aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, while Ukraine reportedly ran out of munitions for its U.S.-made Patriot air defenses earlier in October 2026. Iyer said 2027 is a really big year both geopolitically and for the company's ability to keep momentum as a business. Over the next year or two, Watchtower will focus on succeeding and expanding in its pilot programs.

stories.Headline: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.
stories.Summary:
On October 21, 2026, Josh Longenecker published a guide on profiling TorchNeuron, the open source PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium chips. The article explains how to use torch.profiler with NeuronConfig to capture traces and how to read the key_averages table to compare CPU and Neuron device time. It also shows how Neuron Explorer follows an operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution. The walkthrough profiles three versions of RMSNorm, a naive implementation, the built-in torch.rms_norm function, and a torch.compile version.

The profiling results show that the naive RMSNorm spends most of its Neuron device time on three aten::mul calls, along with aten::mean, aten::add, and aten::rsqrt operations. In contrast, both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse the operation into one kernel dispatch, taking about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. In the example runs, the compiled version took 375 microseconds compared with 403 microseconds for the built-in function. The fused approaches avoid materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

A separate AWS article from October 19, 2026 describes how Deepgram worked with the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering team to port its Nova-3 speech-to-text model to AWS Trainium2. Deepgram serves more than 200,000 developers and 1,400 organizations, processing quadrillions of audio tokens a year. The teams used TorchNeuron in eager mode first, then compiled the encoder and decoder as separate static-shape graphs with torch.compile. They replaced several layers with fused kernels from the public NKI Library, including fused QKV projections, fused feed-forward network layers, and depthwise 1D convolution.

The optimization work used Neuron Explorer for profiling and the Neuron Agentic Development toolkit for analysis and kernel writing. A hand-tuned feed-forward network kernel achieved 2.0 times lower latency than the reference kernel at batch size 96, while a rewritten depthwise conv1d kernel reached a 1.5 times speedup at the same batch size. A custom conv2d kernel unlocked batch sizes above 32 and delivered up to 50 times speedup on the convolution module at batch sizes of 32 or less. The final configuration runs eight model replicas on a single Amazon EC2 trn2.3xlarge instance, processing 11 to 70 percent more audio per dollar than Deepgram's previous compute options.

stories.Headline: Jim Cramer and Ken Fisher’s AI Pick: Microsoft (MSFT)
stories.Summary:
Microsoft stock has moved little over the past year, rising only about 2 percent, and the company reports its fiscal 2027 first quarter results on October 28. Jim Cramer and billionaire Ken Fisher rank Microsoft second on their list of top AI stocks. Microsoft earns AI revenue mainly through Microsoft 365 Copilot, which passed 30 million paid seats in the fiscal fourth quarter, and through Azure, whose revenue grew 43 percent in that quarter. Microsoft also holds a stake in OpenAI, whose products run on Azure first.

The company faces several questions ahead of earnings. Bloomberg reported that Microsoft restricted new cloud subscriptions at key data center hubs in the US and Europe because it lacked capacity. Morgan Stanley estimates Microsoft added about 3.25 gigawatts of capacity in fiscal 2026 and expects about 4.25 gigawatts in fiscal 2027. Microsoft unveiled its Maia 300 AI chip this month, saying it delivers 40 percent more output per megawatt than leading GPU based systems, with production starting early next year.

The commercial backlog rose 84 percent, or 25 percent without OpenAI, and Microsoft plans to spend between 175 billion and 190 billion dollars on capital expenditure in 2026. Morgan Stanley rates Microsoft Overweight and wants to see Azure growth in the mid 40s, better monetization of Microsoft 365 and Copilot, and disciplined operating expenses. The firm says the stock faces a higher bar because it has rebounded in recent weeks and is up about 40 percent over the past six months. Microsoft has beaten earnings estimates in each of the last four quarters, and the market will want to see a fifth.

Recent announcements from partners such as Bloomberg Law, Trellis, Wood Mackenzie, Resilinc and Tucuvi show Microsoft Copilot and Azure being embedded directly into legal, energy, healthcare and supply chain workflows. Analysts expect revenues of 570 billion dollars and earnings of 216.7 billion dollars by 2029, which corresponds to 19.8 percent yearly revenue growth and an earnings increase of about 83 billion dollars from 133.7 billion dollars today. More cautious analysts were assuming about 508.6 billion dollars in revenue and 204.6 billion dollars in earnings by 2029, with a lower price to earnings ratio of 20.9 times, reflecting concern that heavy AI capital spending could weigh on returns. If Azure grows 44 to 45 percent or faster and Copilot use deepens, the rally has support, but if Azure growth falls short, capacity limits persist or OpenAI news hits the backlog, the AI spending worry that sent shares down after the fiscal 2026 third quarter report could return.

stories.Headline: Article Series: Agentic AI Architecture
stories.Summary:
Intel announced technical details for its GPU D-series, formerly code named Crescent Island, on October 12 at the Open Compute Project Global Summit in San Jose. The card is built on the Xe3P architecture and delivers 1.3 petaflops of FP8 compute within a 350 watt, air cooled PCIe form factor. It supports up to 480 GB of LPDDR5X memory at 1.5 TB/s of bandwidth, enough to serve models up to 300 billion parameters on a single card. An 8 GPU system can serve more than 1 trillion parameters, according to Intel's figures.

The Intel branded card carries 160 GB, while ODM partners can configure up to 480 GB. Customer sampling is underway, and Intel showed first silicon alongside a liquid cooled OAM prototype that packs two GPUs per module and eight modules per standard 5U chassis. Intel also introduced Xeon based agentic rack designs with ecosystem partners, many on the OCP Open Rack v3 standard, with select Xeon 6+ configurations exceeding 46,000 cores per rack at 133.45 kW. The Intel AI for Enterprise Agent Toolkit, which uses Xeon to classify prompts, route requests, and orchestrate resources across heterogeneous compute, is available on GitHub. Intel announced Day 0 support for Meta's Muse Glimmer model on both D-series and Xeon.

Nicolas Dubé, Corporate Vice President of the Data Center Systems and Solutions Group at Intel, said open models are expanding the options enterprises have for deploying AI. His keynote framed the goal as putting every prompt in its place. Intel's analysis found that from Llama 2 70B to Kimi K2 1T, the bytes a server must house grew 7.5 times while the bytes read per token fell 4.4 times. Intel's OCP Expo session showed that a single agent turn spends only 30 to 40 percent of its time on the model call, with the remaining 60 to 70 percent being CPU work such as tool execution, data services, and orchestration.

Futurum projects inference focused accelerators will grow from roughly half of CY2025 accelerator spending to 73 percent by CY2030. Agent and reasoning first inference alone is expected to reach 546 billion dollars, or 45 percent of a 1.2 trillion dollar data center semiconductor market, according to Futurum's 1H 2026 forecast. Cautions remain that the part is still in bring up, general availability and pricing are undisclosed, and Intel's accelerator track record after Ponte Vecchio and Gaudi obliges skepticism until production systems ship. The D-Series architecture disclosed at Hot Chips 2026 shows Intel optimizing for memory capacity per dollar where competitors optimize for bandwidth.

stories.Headline: Tokyo stocks fall on AI growth concerns, caution ahead of earnings - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
Tokyo stocks ended lower on Tuesday, Oct. 20, as concerns about the sustainability of artificial intelligence driven growth weighed on investor sentiment. The benchmark Nikkei 225 fell 841.28 points, or 1.30 percent, to 64,075.42. The broader Topix index dropped 58.27 points, or 1.43 percent, to 4,009.21. Selling spread across many shares, with AI and semiconductor related stocks staying weak. Investors were worried about mounting debt at major U.S. data center operator CoreWeave Inc., whose shares fell 8.30, or 11.91 percent, to 61.39.

They were also reluctant to buy on dips ahead of corporate earnings reports due later in October. Rising West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures, linked to concerns over global energy supplies from Middle East tensions, added to the cautious mood. Analysts said these pressures punished weaker balance sheets while leaving room for financially sound, earnings driven companies. A separate report on Oct. 18 highlighted three AI related stocks with expected earnings growth over 33 percent. Advanced Micro Devices, valued at about 863.2 billion dollars, generates most of its revenue from its Data Center segment at about 22.2 billion dollars.

USA Rare Earth, valued at about 4.0 billion dollars, focuses on mining and processing rare earth oxides for magnets, defense systems, semiconductors, data centers, and clean energy hardware. Palantir Technologies, valued near 447 billion dollars, builds data and AI platforms for government and commercial clients, with government revenue at about 3.2 billion dollars and commercial revenue at roughly 2.9 billion dollars. The report said Palantir has zero debt and a large cash position, while AMD expects expanding high performance and AI computing markets sized at about 2 trillion dollars by 2030. USA Rare Earth received an award through the Department of Energy's Critical Materials Innovation, Efficiency and Alternatives program to advance a pilot scale rare earth element separations project in the United States. The articles did not say what would happen next in Tokyo trading beyond the caution ahead of earnings reports.

stories.Headline: FSU Law to examine free speech in the age of AI
stories.Summary:
Florida State University College of Law is partnering with the First Amendment Foundation to host a symposium called “Free Speech in the Age of AI” on Thursday, October 22. The event will bring legal scholars, practitioners, and technology experts to Tallahassee for an afternoon of discussion about free speech and government accountability. It is part of FSU Discovery Days, a weeklong celebration of research, creativity, and discovery taking place through October 17 to 24. The symposium will be held in the College of Law’s Main Classroom Building, Room 101.

Registration opens at 1 p.m., and the program begins at 1:30 p.m. In-person attendance is free, with advance registration requested due to limited seating. Online attendance is available for $99 through separate registration. Faculty from FSU and universities across the country will be joined by representatives from the Freedom of the Press Foundation and the Florida Center for Government Accountability for three panel discussions. Topics will include the use of facial recognition technology to monitor protests and public demonstrations, public access to records related to government AI systems, and legal remedies available when automated decisions infringe on constitutional rights.

Erin O’Hara O’Connor, dean of the FSU College of Law, said people need to understand how the government uses artificial intelligence and what legal protections apply when those uses affect their rights. She said the college is pleased to partner with the First Amendment Foundation to bring scholars and practitioners together to examine these questions and what they mean for the public. Bob Shaw, board chair of the First Amendment Foundation, said the public should be able to understand how government decisions are made, including when artificial intelligence is involved. He said the symposium will examine what access to government records looks like when those records involve AI and how people can seek answers about decisions that affect them.

The event comes as artificial intelligence changes how government agencies conduct surveillance, make decisions, and communicate with the public, and the symposium will examine what those changes mean for the First Amendment and the public’s right to know. The First Amendment Foundation is a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization that advocates for free speech, a free press, and open government in Florida. Through education, training, and advocacy, it helps Floridians understand and exercise their rights to access public records and government meetings. Additional information and registration are available on the event registration page.

stories.Headline: Europe startups weigh relocation as AI regulation and funding gaps strain growth
stories.Summary:
Tanuja Randery, the managing director for Amazon Web Services in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, told Reuters on Wednesday that regulatory hurdles, funding shortages and gaps in workforce skills are pushing European startups to consider relocating. She spoke in an interview with the Reuters Global Markets Forum. Europe has struggled to narrow the gap with the United States and China in the AI race because of tighter regulations, energy constraints and concerns about data privacy. The region has produced few frontier AI models of its own and depends instead on companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

Randery said European businesses report they could spend as much as 40 cents of every euro on regulatory compliance instead of technology. She said nearly 4 in 10 European startups would consider leaving the region to scale, citing an AWS survey of companies, and that among the fastest-growing ones the share is over half. She said startups are reconsidering locations because they want funding and support and are not getting enough funding in Europe. While more than half the businesses in Europe are using AI, she said only one in five are clear about an AI strategy, have an AI governance model and are invested in processes that would fundamentally reshape operations.

Randery said inferencing is where European businesses need to invest, describing it as the process of running trained AI models to generate outputs and the stage at which models are deployed for real-world use. She said Europe needs to go faster and that the choice is not progress versus safety, calling it an "and," not an "or." The articles say tech majors are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into frontier research and scaling AI infrastructure, while Europe's efforts have been limited by the European Union's AI Act, widely seen as the world's most stringent AI regulatory framework. Severe energy and grid constraints are also stymieing progress, according to the articles.

stories.Headline: Using Machine Learning to Predict Microphysical Properties of Cloud Ice Crystals
stories.Summary:
Researchers developed a framework to predict the 3D microphysical properties of ice crystals from 2D images taken inside real clouds, according to a study reported on October 20, 2026 by the Department of Energy Office of Science. The team first generated synthetic ice crystals using 3D modeling software and geometric parameters estimated from the Ice Cryo-Encapsulation Balloon campaign, known as ICEBall. ICEBall was a 2021 field campaign run by the DOE Atmospheric Radiation Measurement Office of Science User Facility. To build the synthetic crystals for their machine learning pipeline, the researchers used scanning electron microscopy to measure real ice crystal samples from ICEBall.

The synthetic crystals trained machine learning models to predict mass, surface area, and the number of spikes of individual crystals. On unseen synthetic images, the models accurately predicted these ice crystal properties. The work offers a machine learning driven framework for estimating ice microphysical properties from in-cloud imagery. The findings could enable downstream constraints on microphysical parameterizations, such as the relationship between mass and size, and help improve how clouds are represented in computer models of the Earth's atmosphere.

The research was funded by the National Science Foundation through the Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics Science and Technology Center. Support also came from the DOE Atmospheric System Research program, and the work drew on the State University of New York at Albany's Atmospheric Sciences Research Center Extreme Collaboration, Innovation, and Technology, or xCITE. The team also received computing support from the Derecho and Casper systems provided by the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research. The study appears in JGR: Machine Learning & Computation.

Separately, Hannah Guan, a fourth-year applied math concentrator at the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, spent a summer at Microsoft Research helping develop machine learning algorithms to better predict subseasonal weather and precipitation patterns. She continued the work after the internship and became first author on a publication in Nature. The project focused on correcting existing forecasts by finding potential errors in how a forecast was made and using machine learning to remove them. Guan said the approach means the team does not have to build something extremely large and compute intensive, and that the method is adaptable because it can correct forecasts from any existing weather model.

stories.Headline: Samsung Electro-Mechanics wins KRW360.5 billion memory substrate deal as AI demand drives expansion
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electro-Mechanics said in a regulatory filing on Oct. 19 that it signed a 360.5 billion won contract to supply package substrates for memory semiconductors to a major global company. The contract runs from Jan. 1 to Dec. 31, 2027. It represents 3.2% of the company's consolidated revenue last year. The agreement marks the company's first disclosed long-term agreement for package substrates. The deal brings the company's total number of disclosed long-term agreements this year to seven.

The contracts were previously concentrated in the components business involving silicon capacitors, multilayer ceramic capacitors and inductors, and have now expanded to the Package Solution division. The cumulative contract value stands at approximately 4.3 trillion won. Samsung Electro-Mechanics produces flip-chip ball grid array and ball grid array substrates through its Package Solution division. A Samsung Electro-Mechanics official said growth in the AI and HPC markets has increased the importance of high-performance package substrates. The official said the company will continue to strengthen its competitiveness in package substrates by expanding supply cooperation with customers and establishing a stable supply system.

Growing demand for high-value products, including substrates for GPUs and CPUs used in AI servers, as well as heterogeneous integration chiplets, is believed to have led to the long-term agreement. Samsung Electro-Mechanics is expanding production capacity to meet rising demand for AI and high-performance computing. Last month, the company disclosed plans to invest 4.27 trillion won in its FC-BGA production facilities in Sejong and 2.51 trillion won in package substrate manufacturing equipment in Vietnam. Including investment in expanding its buildings in Vietnam, total spending is expected to exceed 8 trillion won. The company previously announced plans to invest 8 trillion won at its Sejong facility and 15 trillion won at its Busan facility by 2040 as part of a government-led megaproject.

stories.Headline: Websites go dark worldwide as AI exposes critical security flaws
stories.Summary:
Government agencies and companies around the world shut down websites on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, after two critical flaws were disclosed in PHP, the programming language that underpins many websites. The flaws could let attackers take over web servers without a password. The U.S. National Security Agency urged organizations to patch vulnerable systems or take them offline. PHP volunteers released a fix the same day, but leaked details a day earlier prompted precautionary shutdowns in several countries.

PHP runs about 70 percent of the world's websites, according to an estimate by the security firm Wiz, which described the flaws as among the most severe found in PHP. The NSA said the flaws often provide a direct path to a server's file system or database. Security firm Calif found the flaws in August using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model during an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP's code, and Wiz later found them independently with help from Google's Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol. The flaws were reported privately to PHP developers while a fix was prepared, but details leaked online Tuesday, one day before the planned fix release.

The PHP Foundation, which funds developers working on the language, said in a blog post that anyone running PHP must update now. Volker Dusch, a security engineer at the foundation, told the Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem PHP had faced in more than a decade, comparing it to Heartbleed, a 2014 flaw that set off a worldwide rush to patch. OpenAI said on X that it considered the bug one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory and that it marks a new phase in which AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact. Ethan Mollick, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School who studies AI, wrote on X that companies he talks to are struggling to keep up with the pace of patches needed to shield from AI-driven cyberattacks, and that consumers will now have the same experience of getting everything updated often and fast.

In France, local government websites, including one for Paris police, have been inaccessible since Wednesday afternoon at the request of the French National Cybersecurity Agency, the interior ministry said. In the Netherlands, the national digital identity service DigiD, the website of the House of Representatives and the site of the national cybersecurity center went offline as a precaution, according to Dutch public broadcaster NOS. Belgium's foreign ministry temporarily took its websites offline as a precaution, it said on X, although the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium had recorded no attacks on Belgian sites. In Australia, the Australian Signals Directorate said its own cyber.gov.au site was among government websites affected by the flaws, according to public broadcaster ABC. The discovery came amid a surge in software security disclosures driven by increasingly powerful AI models, with the number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 on track to roughly double last year's record total.

Articles.Title: Websites go dark worldwide as AI exposes critical security flaws
Government websites go dark after AI-discovered flaw sparks security scramble

stories.Headline: US bans DeepSeek across federal agencies, putting AI supply chains under scrutiny
stories.Summary:
The US Secretary of Homeland Security issued an order banning all DeepSeek products and services from federal agencies. The order was reported on October 20, 2026, and it requires government organizations to purge DeepSeek from their IT systems within 60 days. Agencies with what the order calls a compelling justification can request an exemption in writing from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The Department of Homeland Security cited concerns about the Chinese-hosted model, including data sovereignty, lax Chinese laws, and security vulnerabilities.

The ban covers all technology developed by China-based Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co. It also covers affiliated products and any third-party tools or software built using DeepSeek implementations. Affected civilian executive branch agencies include the Departments of Treasury, State, and Justice, but the order does not apply to private consumers, the general public, state and local governments, or Department of Defense national security systems. The order stated that DeepSeek's servers are in the People's Republic of China, whose legal system gives the government extensive authority to access private infrastructure. It also said DeepSeek's account process collects personally identifiable information and may track users, and that its models may contain malware or other vulnerabilities. DHS pointed to open-source security research published in February 2025 that found many iOS mobile apps with critical vulnerabilities.

Analyst Erik Avakian, technical counselor at Infotech, said organizations using hosted AI services may send intellectual property and sensitive data into an environment where they have little visibility or control. He said it is not fair to call every DeepSeek model inherently malicious, but questions remain about data privacy, access under Chinese laws, and susceptibility to jailbreaks. He advised enterprises to approach DeepSeek like any other software supply chain decision and to start with low-risk use cases in a sandboxed environment. He also said the order's coverage of third-party products matters because organizations may use DeepSeek indirectly without knowing what operates underneath.

The ban came as DeepSeek was open-sourcing DeepInfer, its in-house inference framework, which powers DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. In January 2025 the company leaked more than one million log entries, including chat histories and API secrets, through an unsecured database, and DeepSeek reportedly addressed the exposure. Avakian said enterprises should revisit AI inventories, update procurement requirements, and expand third-party risk management. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the 60-day removal requirement and the written exemption process.

stories.Headline: BULL SAS: Bull and CRA join forces to build the Czech AI Gigafactory for Central and Eastern Europe
stories.Summary:
On 21 October 2026, Bull and České Radiokomunikace (CRA) signed a strategic Memorandum of Understanding to combine their expertise and develop a sovereign AI offering for the Czech Republic and Central and Eastern Europe. The agreement was announced in Paris and Prague. It is the first industrial agreement announced under the bilateral strategic cooperation agreement on AI and digital technology signed by Anne Le Hénanff, Minister Delegate for Artificial Intelligence of the French Republic, and Karel Havlíček, Minister of Industry and Trade of the Czech Republic. The partnership strengthens the consortium led by CRA in its candidacy under the European AI Gigafactories programme.

The Czech AI Gigafactory initiative is open to companies from nine Central and Eastern European countries under the Prague declaration: the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Poland, Croatia, Hungary, Lithuania, Latvia, Slovenia and Romania. The consortium aims to maximise the share of European technologies across its infrastructure and AI stack. Bull's manufacturing capabilities in the Czech Republic and France, in partnership with Foxconn, could enable the consortium to build the Gigafactory's computing servers in both countries, with the ambition to integrate European chips as they become available. The open-source-based BullSequana AI platform, developed by teams in Prague, Brno and France, will let organisations develop and deploy AI applications, supported by more than 200 DataSentics AI engineers in the Czech Republic. Bull also intends to reserve Gigafactory capacity for its own clients.

Emmanuel Le Roux, CEO of Bull, said AI Gigafactories are where the company's hardware, AI software and expertise in real-world AI applications come together. He said joining the Czech consortium is an important step in Bull's European AI strategy and strengthens Czech-French cooperation, building on the 200 DataSentics engineers in Prague and Brno. He described the kind of AI Bull wants to build in Europe as open, sustainable and sovereign, giving organisations greater control over their technology and data. Miloš Mastník, CEO of CRA, said the ambition is to build an ecosystem in the Czech Republic that combines computing infrastructure with the development and practical use of artificial intelligence. He said the Memorandum with Bull opens opportunities for cooperation in hardware and software, the two key components of an AI Gigafactory, and that international and Czech companies, public administrations and researchers should be able to develop their own AI solutions there, helping the Czech Republic become a major centre for artificial intelligence in Europe.

AI Gigafactories are intended to strengthen Europe's resilience and capacity to develop and deploy advanced AI at scale, providing computing infrastructure, services and expertise to companies, research organisations and public administrations while helping Europe retain greater control over its data, technologies and strategic AI capabilities. Bull brings end-to-end AI capabilities to the consortium, and its experience in energy efficient supercomputing includes Direct Liquid Cooling and workload-level energy monitoring, while the BullSequana AI platform routes routine tasks to right-sized open models to reduce cost and energy consumption. Bull's dual role as technology provider and future user gives it a direct interest in the Gigafactory's utilisation and long-term success. CRA operates eight data centres and its own fibre-optic backbone network, already provides GPU computing capacity in the Czech Republic, and is developing the AIGF CZ project for Central and Eastern Europe as part of the European AI Gigafactory initiative.

stories.Headline: N.J. schools are wrestling with how teachers and students should use AI in the classroom
stories.Summary:
New Jersey public schools are weighing how generative artificial intelligence should be used in classrooms, and districts are deciding how and when the technology may be used rather than banning it outright. Haddonfield adopted a sweeping AI policy in August that set three tiers of use based on grade level, banning AI in elementary schools while allowing supervised access for middle and high school students. Cherry Hill considered a proposal that would have let parents opt their children out of using AI, but the district backed away from it. Schools across the country are also tackling the issue, and New York City, the nation's largest public school system, placed strict limits on digital devices and AI tools for younger students last month.

Haddonfield, which enrolls about 2,700 students, had only a provision in its academic integrity guidelines requiring students to cite AI as a source before the new policy. The district's policy bans younger students from using AI so they learn foundational and critical learning skills, and all students will get AI literacy education beginning in first grade. Beginning in sixth grade, students can use a Google AI platform called Gemini Notebook, the district's only approved generative AI platform, where teachers can monitor interactions in real time. Cherry Hill's board approved a revised policy on Oct. 13, and teachers there must inform students in writing when generative AI is acceptable for an assignment, using a scale of 0 to 4, with no AI allowed for pre-K and kindergarten. Glassboro adopted MagicSchool as its platform and does not restrict AI use by grade level, though it has mostly been used in middle and high school.

Gino Priolo, a Haddonfield assistant superintendent, said the district needed a policy that protected privacy and provided guidance about safe and appropriate use, and that avoiding AI would mean putting heads in the sand. Cherry Hill Superintendent Kwame Morton said the process was deliberate and rolled out slowly and responsibly, and that the district wants students to be safe and understand how to use the tools responsibly. Allison Staffin, Cherry Hill's director of curriculum and instruction, said the teacher determines which tool is used and what prompts or answers students can generate. Glassboro Superintendent Alfred Lewis said the district is not even seeking to use AI at the elementary level, and he supports a bill by Assemblywoman Heather Simmons, a Gloucester County Democrat, that would prohibit the state's nearly 600 public schools from replacing teachers with AI.

Sarah Schneider Kavanagh, an associate professor at the University of Pennsylvania's Graduate School of Education, said everybody is wrestling with the challenge and called it an enormous paradigm shift for education. Cherry Hill parent Carolina Bevad said she was disappointed in the policy and called it half-baked, and she believes elementary schoolers should be excluded from using AI. Subodha Kumar, a professor at Temple University's Fox School of Business, said bans may not stop students from using AI and that it may take years to determine the best approach. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the policies already adopted and the bill Simmons introduced.
